By the seventh century, Latin-speaking populations east of the Adriatic had significantly diminished, as noted by [PDF p. 169]: "By the seventh century this Roman element was rapidly vanishing." By 620 CE, [PDF p. 170] observes "not a tenth" spoke Latin, leaving only Slavonic principalities and Dalmatian seaports preserving Latin traces.

Emperor Constantine’s policies mandated care for abandoned children, while [PDF p. 173] notes Justinian’s legislation condemned "the characteristic evils of ancient slavery," permitting intermarriage between slaves and freemen. However, [PDF p. 174] argues monastic withdrawal from civic duties hampered imperial defense, with [PDF p. 175] stating "the monastery did not devote itself... to sending out preachers," causing societal neglect. The author explicitly evaluates this withdrawal as harmful, noting [PDF p. 175] how "monastic impulse was working on such a large scale" that it "positively dangerous" to the empire’s stability. The passage concludes [PDF p. 176] by acknowledging Christianity’s dual impact: it "improved the condition of all unhappy classes" yet fostered apathy toward imperial defense during barbarian invasions.
